title: Third objection: grace would give only the powers, not the willing and doing (Philippians 2:13)
source_text: XXXIX. Adde quod si gratia divina sic tantum homines movet, praeparat & incitat ad volendum & perficiendum ea quae Deus jubet, ut tamen ipsum velle & perficere, ea posita, possit in homine non sequi, & de facto saepe non sequatur, operatur illa quidem in homine vires seu dispositiones necessarias ad bonum volendum & perficiendum, non autem ipsum velle & perficere. Sed Apostolus contra testatur, Deum esse qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere pro bona voluntate. Phil. 2. 13.
pass_a_gloss: Add that if divine grace only so moves, prepares and incites men to willing and performing those things which God commands, that yet the very willing and performing, it being posited, can fail to follow in man, and in fact often does not follow, it works indeed in man the powers or dispositions necessary to willing and performing good, but not the very willing and performing. But the Apostle on the contrary testifies, That it is God who works in us both to will and to perform according to his good will. Phil. 2. 13.
pass_b_english: Moreover, if God's grace merely moves, prepares and stirs people to will and to carry out what he commands, in such a way that the willing and doing themselves can fail to follow in a person once grace is given, and in fact often do fail, then grace produces in a person the strength or the dispositions needed for willing and doing good, but not the willing and doing themselves.
The Apostle testifies the opposite: it is God who works in us both to will and to do for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
